name: Dhow / Uru Museum (Beypore Dhow Museum)
tagline: A compact museum celebrating Beypore’s centuries‑old uru (dhow) shipbuilding tradition
summary: Small private museum in Beypore that displays models, tools and stories of the traditional uru (dhow) craft and connects visitors to active shipyards nearby.
description: The Dhow / Uru Museum in Beypore is a privately run display space dedicated to the region’s historic uru — the large wooden dhows built on the Malabar coast. It brings together models, navigational instruments, tools and archival images to explain how these vessels were made and used.

The museum matters because Beypore’s living shipyards remain one of the last places in India where large wooden dhows are hand‑built; the museum acts as an accessible introduction before you visit the working yards and shoreline where urus are constructed.

Visitors leave with a close sense of craft: scale models, old tools (compasses, blocks, winches and other nautical gear) and company histories that link local carpentry, Gulf trade and coastal life. The museum is best seen as part of a short heritage walk that includes the beach, Pulimuttu breakwater and the active shipyards along the Chaliyar estuary.

Practical displays are supplemented by the living landscape — from the museum you can often see or reach sites where full‑scale urus are under construction, making the visit useful for both heritage tourists and those interested in maritime craft.
highlights: Models and scale reconstructions showing hull shapes and joinery
Collections of traditional shipbuilding tools and navigational instruments
Close access to working uru shipyards and the Chaliyar estuary
A private, locally maintained museum reflecting Beypore’s shipwright families
Context for Kerala’s marine trade links with the Gulf and Arabian Sea

sections.heading: Background
body: Beypore has built urus (large wooden dhows) for centuries; the craft links shipwright families, timber trades and Gulf markets. The Dhow/Uru Museum is a private initiative associated with one of the town’s long‑standing shipbuilding firms and collects instruments, photos and models that document that tradition.

The uru remains a living heritage in Beypore: while fewer ships are built today than in earlier centuries, yards along the BC Road–Kakkadath and Pattarmadu continue construction and large vessels still leave for Gulf ports. Government and tourism programmes have recently highlighted Beypore’s uru as a heritage tourism asset.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Inside the museum you find scale models, period photographs, compasses, binoculars and old rigging elements that explain hull forms and traditional joinery. Staff or local guides often explain how planking, caulking and the massive hauling operations work.

Combine the museum visit with a short walk or tuk‑tuk ride to the shipyards and the Pulimuttu breakwater. Watching an uru under construction (from permitted viewing points) gives you a sense of scale you cannot get from models alone.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: The museum is in Beypore, about 10–12 km south of Kozhikode city; allow a half‑day to include the beach and yards. The museum is privately managed and does not always follow fixed public opening hours — confirm before you travel and ask locally for opening times or a guide.

Respect working sites: do not enter yards or climb on vessels without permission, ask before photographing workers, and avoid visiting during heavy monsoon rains when access and working schedules change.

latest.text: Journal reports highlight continuing uru construction in Beypore and renewed interest in promoting the craft for maritime‑heritage tourism.
Tourism Minister P. A. Mohamed Riyas visited Beypore uru yards as part of plans to revive the uru sector and promote tourism‑linked initiatives.
Kerala’s 2026–27 state budget earmarks INR 5 crore for the ‘Beypore Uru Tourism’ project to link the uru industry with tourism and infrastructure improvements.

visitorInfo.bestTime: November to February (cooler, dry weather; calmer seas for yard visits).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Beypore is 10–12 km south of Kozhikode city. Reach Kozhikode by train or flight, then take a taxi or local bus to Beypore; the town is walkable and tuk‑tuks/autorickshaws connect the museum, beach and shipyards.
etiquette: Confirm museum opening hours locally — it is privately run and hours vary.
Ask permission before photographing workers or entering working yards; use guided visits where available.
Wear sturdy shoes for yard/shoreline visits and carry sun/rain protection depending on season.
Combine the museum with a visit to the active shipyards and Pulimuttu breakwater for full context.
